title: Implementation (Chapter 12, Humanity Amplified)
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: In this chapter from Humanity Amplified, Bauschard argues that schools reflexively treat AI as a procedural or purchasing decision, name a director of AI, write an acceptable-use policy, send a memo, and that this answers the wrong question. The real challenge is not technological but human: whether the gains of a transformative technology are shared depends on values and choices about who gets trained, who gets access, and how returns are distributed. He urges districts to begin not with software but with purpose, starting with an honest, organization-wide conversation about mission and readiness before buying or banning anything.
points: Treating AI as a procedural or purchasing decision, a director, a policy, a memo, answers the wrong question and repeats the fate of the interactive whiteboard.
The tool in front of a school is a prototype; the world it points to is the real assignment, and that world is a human problem, not a technology problem.
Whether AI's gains are shared depends on values and choices, who gets trained, who gets access, how returns are distributed, not on any economic law.
Schools that begin with the software and back into purpose repeat past reform mistakes; schools that begin with purpose have a chance.
Before buying or banning anything, a district should locate itself honestly on a readiness ladder (unaware, aware, ready, competent), where honesty matters more than the rung.
quotes: When a technology this large lands on a school, the reflex is procedural: name a director of AI, write an acceptable-use policy, send a memo, and move on. Treat it as a purchasing decision and it goes in the same drawer as the interactive whiteboard.
The tool in front of you is a prototype. The world it points to is the assignment. And that world is not, at bottom, a technology problem. It is a human one.
Whether the gains are shared depends on values and choices — on who gets trained, who gets access, and how the returns are distributed.
Schools that begin with the software and back into the purpose tend to repeat the mistakes of every reform that came before them. Schools that begin with the purpose have a chance.

Before a district buys anything or bans anything, it should talk — across the whole organization — about what it values, what it is trying to do, what stands in the way, and what it owes the people it serves.
A district that calls itself “aware” when it is really “unaware” will plan for a building it doesn’t have.
